sections.heading: Admitting the anger I need to repent of
sections.text: Holy Lord, there is so little real repentance in the world, and there is so much in me that needs it. I am especially troubled by my anger—by the ugliness of it, the harm it does, and the way it rises in me so quickly. I do not want to keep giving it room. I come to you because I cannot conquer it by willpower. Please give me strength to turn from it for good.
theological_themes: Sinful anger is not a small personality flaw but a real evil before God.
Repentance includes both honest grief over sin and a serious desire to turn from it.
Lasting change requires God’s help, not self-reliance.

scripture_references.connection: James directly warns believers that human anger does not produce the righteousness God desires. This supports the prayer’s confession that uncontrolled anger is spiritually serious, not merely socially inconvenient.
The psalmist asks God to search and expose the heart in order to be led away from grievous ways. That fits the prayer’s willingness to let God uncover the sin beneath angry reactions.

sections.heading: Refusing to excuse my outbursts
sections.text: I know how easy it is to make excuses. I tell myself it came on suddenly, that I did not enjoy it, that I felt bad afterward, or that even godly people have failed in the same way. But those excuses do not heal anything. Forgetting an outburst is not repentance. Covering the wound with a quick apology or moving on as if nothing happened will not bring real peace. I need the peace that comes only through Christ’s blood.
theological_themes: Self-justification keeps sin alive by minimizing it.
False peace comes from forgetting, explaining, or covering sin; true peace comes through Christ’s atoning work.
Repentance refuses to treat regret as the same thing as turning to God.

scripture_references.connection: John connects cleansing from sin with the blood of Jesus and with honest confession rather than denial. This grounds the prayer’s rejection of superficial peace and its appeal to Christ for real cleansing.
This proverb contrasts hiding sin with confessing and forsaking it. It supports the prayer’s concern that merely moving past anger without dealing with it before God is not healing.

sections.heading: Seeing the selfishness underneath
sections.text: Lord God, show me the truth about my anger. It usually flares when something blocks what I want, interrupts my plans, wounds my pride, or makes life harder for me. At those moments I am often more concerned with pleasing myself than with pleasing Christ. In every hard thing, there is what crosses me and there is what dishonors you. In every good thing, there is what pleases me and there is what pleases you. My sin is that my heart rises and falls according to what serves me, while I forget what belongs to Christ.
theological_themes: Sinful anger often grows from self-centered desires and frustrated pride.
The believer is called to measure life by Christ’s honor, not personal comfort or preference.
Self-examination asks not only what happened, but what the heart wanted most.

scripture_references.connection: James traces quarrels to disordered desires within the heart. This directly illuminates the prayer’s claim that anger often erupts when self-centered wants are crossed.

Paul says Christ died so that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him. That supports the prayer’s desire to stop measuring circumstances mainly by whether they please the self.

sections.heading: Owning what I have failed to confront
sections.text: I have been too willing to let this sin remain. Like Eli, who failed to deal with sin when he should have, I have often failed to rebuke what is wrong in me. I have treated my anger as understandable instead of bringing it into the light. Lord, I confess it plainly now. I run to the blood of Christ for pardon, cleansing, and peace.
theological_themes: God’s people must not tolerate known sin, even when it is inward and familiar.
Confession brings sin into the light before God instead of allowing it to remain protected.
Pardon and peace are sought in Christ’s sacrifice, not in self-improvement or forgetfulness.

scripture_references.connection: Eli was judged because he knew of sin and failed to restrain it. The prayer applies that warning personally, not as a direct equivalence, but as a call to stop passively tolerating known sin in the heart.
Hebrews teaches that Christ’s blood cleanses the conscience for service to God. This supports the prayer’s appeal to Christ not only for pardon but for inward peace and renewed obedience.

sections.heading: Asking for real repentance that lasts
sections.text: So please give me repentance that is real: a broken heart that does not make peace with sin, a sorrow that leads me back to you, and a contrition that lasts beyond the moment after I lose my temper. You do not despise a broken and humbled heart. Even after this sin, I come to you trusting your mercy, asking you to make me clean and teach me to walk in the patience and gentleness of Christ.
theological_themes: True repentance is a gift from God and produces lasting change.
God receives the contrite rather than despising them.
Christian growth includes learning Christlike patience and gentleness in place of sinful anger.

scripture_references.connection: David teaches that God receives a broken and contrite heart. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that honest repentance is not rejected, even after serious sin.
Paul distinguishes godly grief, which leads to repentance, from worldly sorrow. This supports the prayer’s request for more than temporary regret after an angry outburst.

Paul describes the Spirit’s fruit, including patience, gentleness, and self-control, in contrast to the works of the flesh. This fits the prayer’s plea for God to replace sinful anger with Christlike character.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses “passion” in the older sense of uncontrolled anger; this adaptation renders it as anger and outbursts to avoid confusion with modern meanings of passion.

The prayer treats this anger as sinful because it is self-centered and uncontrolled. Scripture allows for righteous anger, so the adaptation preserves the original focus on anger that arises from pride, self-pleasing, and failure to honor Christ.

The reference to Eli is a strong biblical analogy. The adaptation applies it to the personal failure to confront known sin in one’s own heart, rather than implying the pray-er shares Eli’s exact office, family responsibility, or historical judgment.
significant_interpretive_choices: The original’s image of “skinning over their wound” was rendered as covering the wound with a quick apology or moving on as if nothing happened, preserving the idea of superficial treatment without reproducing the archaic phrasing.

The phrase “double cross” was interpreted to mean that every hardship can be viewed both in relation to how it affects the self and in relation to how it concerns God’s honor. The modern version states this contrast directly.
The prayer’s appeal to “peace in Christ’s blood” was kept as a concrete appeal to Christ’s atoning death, not reduced to a general feeling of emotional relief.
